title: "Offensively cheap": Solar power is looking up
gist: Chinese panel prices falling from $5-$6 per watt around 2000 to roughly 12 cents today have pushed distributed solar to nearly 1.2 terawatts worldwide by end-2025, about three times the global nuclear fleet, with adoption now driven by cost and reliability rather than decarbonization policy in Pakistan, South Africa, India, the Philippines and across Africa. The resulting behind-the-meter shift is eroding utility revenue — Eskom traces roughly 7 percent of an 11.7 TWh sales decline to rooftop solar and batteries — while creating grid-stability and forecast-visibility problems that plug-and-play panels, household batteries, AI forecasting and tariff redesign are all racing to address.

insights.claim: Solar panels that cost $5 to $6 per watt of generation capacity at the turn of the millennium now sell for around 12 cents per watt, a level one think-tank co-founder calls "offensively cheap."
insights.speaker: Financial Times
insights.so_what: A roughly 40-to-50-fold price collapse is the single input driving every downstream disruption here; assume no floor is in sight while Chinese capacity overhangs demand.
insights.quote: Today, they sell for around 12 cents per watt, a level described as “offensively cheap” by Dave Jones, co-founder of think-tank Ember.
insights.locator: At the turn of the millennium, solar panels cost $5-$6 per watt

insights.claim: The price reduction in solar panels is entirely the result of an explosion in China's production capacity, which stands at roughly 1.36 terawatts according to Wood Mackenzie.
insights.speaker: Financial Times
insights.so_what: Chinese manufacturing capacity exceeds global annual demand by a wide margin, so module margins stay compressed and the value migrates to inverters, storage and grid services.
insights.quote: That reduction is entirely the result of an explosion in China’s production capacity, which, according to research firm Wood Mackenzie, stands at roughly 1.36 terawatts
insights.locator: That reduction is entirely the result of an explosion

insights.claim: Beijing is actively trying to rein in solar manufacturing output to combat price deflation, indicating the Chinese state now views panel cheapness as a domestic economic problem.
insights.speaker: Financial Times
insights.so_what: Supply-side discipline from Beijing is the main upside risk to module prices; watch policy signals as the leading indicator for panel cost inflection.
insights.quote: even as Beijing tries to rein in output to combat price deflation
insights.locator: That reduction is entirely the result of an explosion

insights.claim: Distributed solar capacity installed on roofs, in yards, gardens and other land totaled almost 1.2 terawatts worldwide at the end of 2025, roughly three times the size of the global nuclear power fleet.
insights.speaker: Financial Times
insights.so_what: Behind-the-meter capacity is now a nuclear-fleet-scale asset class that sits entirely outside utility control and planning.
insights.locator: At the end of 2025, such capacity totaled almost 1.2 terawatts

insights.claim: Cheap panels moved solar from a subsidized decarbonization technology into a vital electricity source in places where power is scarce, expensive or unreliable, starting in Pakistan, Brazil and South Africa and spreading to Africa and the Philippines.
insights.speaker: Financial Times
insights.so_what: Solar demand has decoupled from climate policy, so US or EU subsidy withdrawal no longer caps global module demand growth.
insights.locator: Cheaper panels enabled a vast rollout in China itself

insights.claim: A cement producer in Chakwal, Pakistan is adding 6.34 megawatts of solar generation by the end of the year on top of 26 MW already installed, with solar already supplying over a quarter of its plant's electricity.
insights.speaker: Financial Times
insights.so_what: Heavy industry in high-power-cost markets is self-generating at scale, structurally removing anchor load from national utilities.
insights.locator: In the badlands of Chakwal, in north-central Pakistan

insights.claim: The general manager of a Pakistani cement plant producing over 3 million tonnes per year says on-site solar is the only way the plant can compete, because rivals have already moved in that direction.
insights.speaker: Abdul Waheed, general manager at Chakwal
insights.so_what: Once one industrial player self-generates, the cost advantage forces the whole sector to follow — adoption is competitive, not voluntary, and therefore fast.
insights.quote: It’s the only way we can compete
insights.locator: It’s the only way we can compete

insights.claim: Africa's biggest supermarket group has been installing panels on roofs and trucks in South Africa and Namibia since 2015 and now controls around 43 megawatts of peak capacity, enough its sustainability head says to power an entire suburb, and is now examining battery storage.
insights.speaker: Financial Times
insights.so_what: Commercial real estate rooftops are becoming utility-scale generation fleets, and the same corporates are the next wave of battery demand.
insights.quote: power an entire suburb
insights.locator: Sanjeev Raghubir, head of sustainability at Shoprite

insights.claim: Most of the roughly 17 gigawatts of new solar Africa is expected to install this year will be small-scale installations at factories and other businesses, because daytime consumption makes solar a natural fit for commercial users.
insights.speaker: Financial Times
insights.so_what: African solar growth is commercial and behind-the-meter, which means it shows up in import statistics rather than in utility procurement pipelines.
insights.quote: If you’re a business, you’re using electricity during the day—it’s a natural fit for you to use solar
insights.locator: Based on analysis of customs data, Ember estimates

insights.claim: In the Philippines rooftop solar capacity may have almost doubled in the 12 months to April, with residential systems now paying for themselves in just over three years.
insights.speaker: Financial Times
insights.so_what: A three-year payback is inside the horizon most households will finance, which is the threshold where adoption goes vertical.
insights.locator: In the Philippines, Ember estimates rooftop solar capacity

insights.claim: The Philippine electricity distributor reported that rooftop solar generated 372 gigawatt hours in the first six months of the year.
insights.speaker: Financial Times
insights.so_what: Distributors are now measuring meaningful volumes of generation they do not own or dispatch, which shows directly in their sales line.
insights.locator: Meralco, the country’s electricity distributor

insights.claim: India's national subsidized rooftop solar program, launched in February 2024 with a budget worth nearly $8 billion at current exchange rates, has installed panels on over 5 million homes and is adding roughly 500,000 homes per month.
insights.speaker: Financial Times
insights.so_what: A run rate of 500,000 homes a month is the largest single residential solar demand pool on earth and a direct volume driver for module and inverter suppliers.
insights.locator: The Indian government’s national subsidized rooftop solar program

insights.claim: The chief executive of an Indian power company frames mass rooftop adoption as a democratization of the use of electricity rather than as a threat to incumbents.
insights.speaker: Praveer Sinha, chief executive of Tata Power
insights.so_what: Incumbent utilities that own the installation business capture the transition instead of being disintermediated by it — the key differentiator among utility equities.
insights.quote: It’s a democratization of the use of electricity
insights.locator: The Indian government’s national subsidized rooftop solar program

insights.claim: A Kenyan company that lends families money for solar and battery installations describes the household step change as going from two or three kerosene lanterns to a daily-use light 20 to 40 times brighter.
insights.speaker: Anish Thakkar, co-founder of Sun King
insights.so_what: Pay-as-you-go solar lending is the consumer-credit business riding this wave; the underlying value proposition displaces kerosene spend, not grid tariffs.
insights.quote: A home goes from burning two or three kerosene lanterns to a light that is 20 to 40 times brighter, [turned] on every day
insights.locator: But solar is also a boon for households

insights.claim: Millions of people in poorer countries now have more reliable electricity access through their own individual installations rather than through massive centralized infrastructure.
insights.speaker: Financial Times
insights.so_what: Electrification is happening without the multi-decade grid capex cycle development finance assumed, undercutting the investment case for large centralized build-outs in frontier markets.
insights.locator: The solar revolution made possible by cheap Chinese photovoltaic panels

themes.theme: Utility revenue erosion and the death spiral

insights.claim: South Africa's state power utility estimates rooftop solar panels and batteries were responsible for around 7 percent of the 11.7 terawatt-hour reduction in its electricity sales for the year ending March.
insights.speaker: Financial Times
insights.so_what: Quantified: behind-the-meter solar is a real but still minority driver of utility volume loss — industrial demand destruction from high prices is the bigger hit.
insights.locator: It estimates that rooftop solar panels and batteries

insights.claim: The utility serving 20 million people in Karachi describes solar panels as both a curse and a blessing because its wealthiest neighborhoods, its best customers, are the ones opting for self-generation.
insights.speaker: Syed Muhammad Taha, chief executive of K-Electric
insights.so_what: Solar defection is adversely selected toward the highest-margin customers, so revenue falls faster than volume does.
insights.quote: These are my best customers
insights.locator: The concrete villas in Karachi’s wealthy Defence Housing Authority

insights.claim: In Karachi's poorer Lyari borough, non-payment rates are so high that the utility loses 30 to 40 rupees for every 100 rupees it spends supplying the area.
insights.speaker: Financial Times
insights.so_what: A 30-40 percent loss rate on the residual customer base is what makes the Pakistani death spiral self-reinforcing once wealthy customers leave.
insights.locator: Those customers not using solar panels in Karachi’s Defence Housing Authority

insights.claim: The overriding task for South Africa's utility is to avoid the kind of utility death spiral already seen in Pakistan, where poorer people end up shouldering a greater proportion of the cost of power infrastructure.
insights.speaker: Financial Times
insights.so_what: Pakistan is the working template for how distributed solar breaks a utility balance sheet; screen emerging-market utility debt against that pattern.
insights.locator: But its overriding task is to avoid the kind of “utility death spiral”

insights.claim: Pakistani households face rising power bills because utilities are recouping the cost of a previous poorly planned build-out of centralized generation capacity, and tenants in rundown buildings often cannot install panels to escape.
insights.speaker: Financial Times
insights.so_what: Stranded centralized capex plus renter exclusion from solar is the mechanism converting an energy transition into a regressive cost shift.
insights.quote: I am spending more than half of my income on power
insights.locator: Customers like Azem Baloch, a mechanic living in Lyari

insights.claim: An Indian utility executive concedes that losing paying consumers while retaining non-paying ones is a genuine problem, but argues the risk is mitigated by targeting support at lower-income households and by earning revenue from installing panels.
insights.speaker: Praveer Sinha, chief executive of Tata Power
insights.so_what: Subsidizing solar for the poor first inverts the adverse-selection problem — a policy design worth watching for replication in other emerging markets.
insights.quote: if paying consumers are going and the non-paying consumers stay with you, then it becomes a problem
insights.locator: Tata Power’s Sinha acknowledges

insights.claim: Utilities must fund grid upkeep and the power stations that fill the gap when it is dark or cloudy even as the customers exporting daytime power reduce the sales revenue that pays for both.
insights.speaker: Financial Times
insights.so_what: The backup fleet becomes a capacity asset serving fewer billable kilowatt hours, which forces the shift from volumetric to fixed network charging.
insights.locator: The lower revenues come as Eskom needs to fund the upkeep of the grid

insights.claim: A research manager at S&P Global frames the core unresolved question as who pays grid charges when solar and batteries keep reducing electricity sales to the grid.
insights.speaker: Josefin Berg, research manager for solar and energy storage at S&P Global
insights.so_what: Grid cost recovery is the central regulatory battleground of the decade and determines whether network operators remain investable.
insights.quote: if you have more and more solar and batteries, reducing the sales of electricity for the grid, who is paying for the grid charges?
insights.locator: Distribution grids may not always be prepared

insights.claim: A power systems professor argued that while solar and other renewables did not directly cause the day-long blackout across much of Spain and Portugal last year, Spain had failed to sufficiently adapt its power system to reflect their growth.
insights.speaker: Professor Janusz Bialek, Imperial College London
insights.so_what: The blackout risk is a system-adaptation failure, not a renewables failure — which means capex on grid re-engineering is the mitigating trade, not slowing solar.
insights.locator: That challenge was dramatically illustrated last year by a day-long blackout

insights.claim: The same professor warns that the rapidly increasing share of renewables causes a profound change in how power systems behave that engineers do not yet fully understand.
insights.speaker: Professor Janusz Bialek, Imperial College London
insights.so_what: Acknowledged model uncertainty at high renewable penetration means tail-risk blackout events are underpriced in both insurance and utility equity.
insights.quote: The rapidly increasing share of renewables in many power systems causes a profound change in the way power systems behave which we do not yet fully understand
insights.locator: The rapidly increasing share of renewables in many power systems

insights.claim: Australian high-voltage transmission operators face the problem of too little demand as consumers draw from rooftop panels, and very low demand makes it harder to run certain power plants needed to keep the system stable.
insights.speaker: Financial Times
insights.so_what: Minimum-demand events, not peak demand, are the emerging operational constraint — they create value for storage, curtailment services and synchronous condensers.
insights.locator: In Australia, operators of the high-voltage transmission system

insights.claim: Energy groups in some Australian states are having to literally give away excess power generated in the middle of the day.
insights.speaker: Financial Times
insights.so_what: Zero or negative midday prices are the direct signal that storage arbitrage economics are improving as solar penetration rises.
insights.locator: energy groups in some states are having to literally give away excess power

insights.claim: Power flowing from local distribution networks back into transmission grids causes voltage increases that limit how much electricity households can actually export.
insights.speaker: Financial Times
insights.so_what: Physical export limits cap the resale value of household solar, strengthening the case for on-site batteries over feeding the grid.
insights.locator: Power flowing from local distribution networks into transmission grids

insights.claim: A power systems professor says a large cloud formation over a city saturated with rooftop solar can cut photovoltaic production so sharply that it looks to the grid like the loss of almost a nuclear power station.
insights.speaker: Pierluigi Mancarella, chair professor of electrical power systems at the University of Melbourne
insights.so_what: Weather now creates instantaneous gigawatt-scale contingency events, which sets the required scale for fast-response reserves and batteries.
insights.quote: If you have a massive cloud formation, the rooftop PV production can drop by so much that it looks like you have lost basically almost a nuclear power station.
insights.locator: Perth, for example, is covered in rooftop solar

insights.claim: A whole country had to rely on its state utility's generation for three consecutive days after prolonged cloudy weather slashed rooftop solar output, showing distributed solar shifts rather than removes the need for centralized capacity.
insights.speaker: Dan Marokane, chief executive of Eskom
insights.so_what: Backup capacity must be sized for multi-day solar droughts, which is why utilities need capacity payments even as energy sales fall.
insights.quote: Three weeks ago… the whole country had to rely on Eskom generation for three days
insights.locator: Everyone who has rooftop solar in any major city, they are still connected to the grid

themes.theme: Plug-and-play panels and the visibility gap

insights.claim: Since the end of August, British households have been able to buy 800-watt plug-in solar panels in supermarkets or DIY stores, with the government framing the move as giving them breathing space on bills.
insights.speaker: Financial Times
insights.so_what: Retail-channel solar turns panels into an impulse-purchase consumer good, opening a new demand channel for grocers and DIY chains.
insights.locator: The fallout from the US-Iran war has led to more interest in rooftop solar in Britain

insights.claim: New Jersey's governor exempted plug-in solar devices from metering requirements while saying she was laser-focused on driving down energy costs, and such panels are proving popular in the US despite the president's antipathy to renewables and his elimination of the rooftop solar tax credit.
insights.speaker: Financial Times
insights.so_what: State-level cost-of-living politics is overriding federal renewable hostility, so US distributed solar demand is more resilient than the tax-credit repeal implies.
insights.locator: Several US states have also been making it easier for households

insights.claim: A power systems professor says adding plug-and-play panels to an already unwieldy system is not a good idea, because a million consumers each adding a kilowatt creates a gigawatt of generation the system operator can barely see.
insights.speaker: Pierluigi Mancarella, chair professor of electrical power systems at the University of Melbourne
insights.so_what: Invisible aggregate capacity is a systemic forecasting risk, and the cheapest fix — mandatory registration — is exactly what regulators are relaxing.
insights.quote: This is not a good idea
insights.locator: But he questions the merits of adding plug-and-play panels

insights.claim: Plug-in solar panels must be registered in most jurisdictions, but research in Germany has shown many installations are not.
insights.speaker: Financial Times
insights.so_what: Registration compliance failure in a high-compliance market like Germany means official distributed capacity figures systematically understate reality.
insights.locator: In most jurisdictions, plug-in solar panels have to be registered

insights.claim: The world's power infrastructure was not designed for solar self-generation, so the influx of ungovernable distributed energy threatens investment models, pricing models and even security of supply.
insights.speaker: Financial Times
insights.so_what: The framing to carry: this is an infrastructure mismatch problem, which means the profit pool shifts to whoever re-engineers grids for two-way flow.
insights.quote: such a massive, ungovernable influx of energy carries risks, too—the world’s power infrastructure was not designed for solar self-generation
insights.locator: But such a massive, ungovernable influx of energy carries risks

insights.claim: Distributed solar is transforming the electricity system from a centralized structure into one where anyone can produce power, while distribution grids may not be prepared to absorb a large influx of electricity.
insights.speaker: Josefin Berg, research manager for solar and energy storage at S&P Global
insights.so_what: Distribution-level upgrades, not transmission, are where the near-term grid capex bottleneck sits.
insights.quote: completely transforming the system from the centralized structure to something where anyone can produce power
insights.locator: Josefin Berg, research manager for solar and energy storage at S&P Global

themes.theme: Mitigations: batteries, AI forecasting and tariff redesign

insights.claim: Household batteries that store rooftop output rather than exporting it are falling in price and will help ease grid absorption problems.
insights.speaker: Financial Times
insights.so_what: Residential storage is the direct beneficiary of both falling battery costs and worsening export limits — a two-sided tailwind.
insights.locator: Household batteries, which allow some of the power generated

insights.claim: The UK government's AI champion for clean energy argued in a report that AI can learn the underlying structure of the grid and speed up the calculations needed to measure supply and demand.
insights.speaker: Lucy Yu, the UK government's AI champion for clean energy
insights.so_what: Grid operations is becoming a named AI application area with government backing, creating a procurement channel for forecasting and optimization vendors.
insights.quote: underlying structure of the grid
insights.locator: So too would better visibility over supply

insights.claim: A UK distribution network operator has just completed a £389,000 study developing machine-learning models to better estimate the solar generation capacity connected to its network.
insights.speaker: Financial Times
insights.so_what: Network operators are paying real money simply to find out what is connected to their own wires — an early, small but expanding software spend line.
insights.locator: UK Power Networks has just finished a £389,000 study

insights.claim: A solar forecasting company retrains its machine learning models every hour, weighting the last hour of grid changes more heavily in spring than a year of history, because seasonal volatility dominates forecast accuracy.
insights.speaker: Jon Ecker, general manager for Europe at Amperon
insights.so_what: Hourly retraining is the emerging technical standard in power forecasting; vendors on slower cycles will lose accuracy-driven contracts.
insights.quote: They know that in springtime, they’re going to need to weigh what has happened over the last hour more heavily than in the last year
insights.locator: Jon Ecker, general manager for Europe at Amperon

insights.claim: New technology developed in Australia can increase the amount of power grids absorb from households, and the lead engineering lesson is not to wait until the last minute because the transition is foreseeable.
insights.speaker: Pierluigi Mancarella, chair professor of electrical power systems at the University of Melbourne
insights.so_what: Australia is the live testbed for high-penetration distributed solar; its hosting-capacity technologies are the export product other grids will buy next.
insights.quote: Engineers are moving very fast to respond [to the changes]. But the major lesson is: don’t wait until the last minute—you know this is coming
insights.locator: New technology developed in Australia can increase

insights.claim: South Africa's utility is redesigning tariffs to separate network costs from energy costs, which analysts expect to make pricing more efficient and help the market adapt to the supply shift.
insights.speaker: Financial Times
insights.so_what: Unbundled network charging is the structural fix for cost recovery; utilities that get it approved first de-risk their revenue base.
insights.locator: The company is redesigning tariffs to distinguish between network and energy costs

insights.claim: South Africa's utility chief is courting heavy electricity users such as data centers and bitcoin miners to reverse falling power sales, while warning that network investment to support renewables will find its way into the electricity price.
insights.speaker: Dan Marokane, chief executive of Eskom
insights.so_what: AI data centers and crypto mining are being recruited as replacement load for utilities losing residential volume — a demand-side pairing to watch across emerging markets.
insights.quote: is going to find its way into the electricity price
insights.locator: Eskom chief Marokane says he is looking to heavy electricity users

insights.claim: Pakistan has slashed the amount grid operators pay households to buy back surplus solar power, while utilities plan large-scale solar and wind plus battery storage to reduce reliance on oil-fired generation after sunset.
insights.speaker: Financial Times
insights.so_what: Cutting feed-in rates is the first lever stressed utilities pull; it shifts household economics decisively toward self-consumption plus storage.
insights.locator: In Pakistan, utilities plan to deploy large-scale solar and wind plants

insights.claim: South Africa's utility has waived registration fees for new solar installations partly to gain visibility over what is being installed, and its chief executive expects uptake to keep rising regardless.
insights.speaker: Dan Marokane, chief executive of Eskom
insights.so_what: Utilities are now paying, in forgone fees, for data rather than fighting adoption — an admission that solar growth cannot be stopped, only observed.
insights.quote: I think we will see more uptake [of solar]
insights.locator: In the meantime, Eskom has waived registration fees

insights.claim: Consumer interest in rooftop solar in Britain rose as fallout from the US-Iran war raised energy cost concerns, linking geopolitical conflict directly to distributed generation demand.
insights.speaker: Financial Times
insights.so_what: Energy-security shocks are now a reliable demand catalyst for distributed solar in rich countries; treat conflict headlines as a solar demand signal.
insights.locator: The fallout from the US-Iran war has led to more interest
